entries.title: Germany: Chancellor Merz is fighting for his political survival
entries.summary: Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt election, many are expressing doubts about Chancellor and party leader Friedrich Merz. But they don't appear to have any viable alternative.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Chancellor Merz tries to rally his troops

September 16, 2026

Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt election, many are expressing doubts about Chancellor and party leader Friedrich Merz. But they don't appear to have any viable alternative.

Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various European countries had gathered there for the Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.

When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent: "That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

Why is Merz so unpopular?

And another heavy defeat looks likely in the state elections coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low seven percent. Failure to clear the five-percent hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The state elections that took place earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt were won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised that he would "cut in half" support for the AfD. Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."

When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese said on the Welt TV channel: "You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now." He added: "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst

But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.

SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April, when state elections will be held in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag. However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the Chancellor."

The eight German state premiers from Merz's CDU have issued a joint statement backing him as pressure mounts over his leadership following the party's election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

The statement was signed by all eight CDU state premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Hendrik Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Pivotal state elections coming up

So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Friedrich Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down. s."

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

His schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources confirmed.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots
entries.summary: US prosecutors accuse the foreign nationals of conducting surveillance, attacks, and murder-for-hire operations for Moscow — just after a DW investigation identified one of the suspects as a salsa teacher in Russia.
entries.content:
United States of America

US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots

September 16, 2026

US prosecutors accuse the foreign nationals of conducting surveillance, attacks, and murder-for-hire operations for Moscow — just after a DW investigation identified one of the suspects as a salsa teacher in Russia.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russianintelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe.

"The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment.

Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, 22, were charged with an alleged conspiracy to commit financial terrorism.

Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.

All the individuals are still at large.

The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot.

The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels.

What else did the DOJ say?

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC.

According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania.

The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident."

Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States.

The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: US announces South Africa visa curbs over race claims
entries.summary: The visa restriction policy targets South African nationals who US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claims are responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white citizens.
entries.content:
South Africa

US announces South Africa visa curbs over race claims

September 16, 2026

The visa restriction policy targets South African nationals who US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claims are responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white citizens.

The United States has announced a new visa restriction policy for South Africans amid continuing claims that the white, Afrikaner minority in the African country is suffering from "race-based discrimination."

US President Donald Trump's administration has ⁠criticized South Africa over a range of issues including land and employment laws that are meant to redress inequalities that Black people still face 30 years after the end of apartheid.

"As President Trump has made clear, the South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed.

"The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked," Rubio said. "These actions directly undermine peace, economic stability, and the rule of law, and they are incompatible with the pillars of America's foreign policy."

The US ambassador ‌to South ⁠Africa ⁠said ​​on ​social media ‌on Wednesday that ‌the visa restrictions were "only the first ⁠step ​in ​a ​series of ‌escalatory measures."

Rubio did not name any individuals to be immediately affected by the restrictions but said they would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa."

South Africa: Discrimination claims based on misinformation

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says there is no evidence of discrimination against white people in his country and has called for global efforts to debunk ⁠false ​stories about white persecution.

Nevertheless, the Trump administration has continued to attack South Africa.

In 2025, Trump berated President Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide" in South Africa. He has also hit the country with high tariffs, boycotted a G20 summit in Johannesburg and launched a special program allowing thousands of white Afrikaners to settle in the United States.

Relations between Washington and Pretoria have also nosedived over South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), in which it accuses the US ally of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
entries.summary: Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close.
entries.content:
BusinessGlobal issues

WEF report: Progress on gender equality remains 'fragile'

September 16, 2026

Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close.

The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%.

However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile."

The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006.

Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.

WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable."

"To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report.

Women still missing in top power roles

The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence.

While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today."

Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms.

For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006.

Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th).

US falls in gender gap ranking

The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed.

The country achieved full parity in education for a second year — ranking first in the world in that area.

In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated.

The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration.

The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president.

India stuck while China moves up

India, the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed.

The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted.

India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%.

In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019.

China, meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers.

Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana

Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking.

Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too.

Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.

However, Africa shows the widest range of outcomes for women, the report found, with Chad recording the lowest score of 57.8% parity closed.

Other large climbers in the 2026 report were Guatemala, which rose 31 points to 50th place, and the Czech Republic, which climbed 25 points to 77th.

The WEF also ranked the countries that have progressed the most since 2006 in closing gender gaps, namely Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, France, Guatemala, Iceland, Mexico, Namibia and Nepal.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
entries.summary: A Hague tribunal ruled that Hashim Thaci, a former leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), is responsible for war crimes carried out during the war of independence with Serbia.
entries.content:
Kosovo

Kosovo ex-president Thaci convicted of war crimes

Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026

A Hague tribunal ruled that Hashim Thaci, a former leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), is responsible for war crimes carried out during the war of independence with Serbia.

A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.

Thaci, a former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention.

He was tried along with three other former KLA guerrilla leaders in The Hague.

What did the tribunal rule?

The tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces at the hands of the KLA during the conflict. He was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people and torturing more than 300 people

The court added Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes."

Prosecutors alleged KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.

This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.

The defense argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.

Lawyers had argued there was no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.

Seen as heroes in Kosovo

The accused are revered as national heroes in Kosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.

The verdict in The Hague was livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters gathered.

This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal.

Foreign embassies warned of the possibility of unrest after the verdict.

"Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.

"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.

After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.

The Kosovo War left 13,000 people dead, of which some 9,000 ethnic Albanian Kosovars who were subjected to a campaign of ethnic cleansing at the hands of Serbian forces. The conflict ended after NATO intervened in 1999, pushing Serbian forces out.

Serbia still does not officially recognize its former province Kosovo as an independent state.

Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo

Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.

During the verdict, the presiding judge, Charles Smith, emphasized that the trial was "not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army" or its goal of Kosovo independence. 

The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.

Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.

Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.

"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
entries.summary: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.
entries.content:
Europe

'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack

September 16, 2026

A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.

A decade after the deadliest jihadist attack in Germany's history, a new six-part TV series looks at the institutional failures that allowed it to happen.

"Blindspot Berlin," which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, follows the year-long police investigation that failed to stop Anis Amri — a Tunisian whose asylum applications had been rejected, and who was already known to German security services — from driving a hijacked truck into a crowded Christmas market at Berlin's Breitscheidplatz on December 19, 2016.

Twelve people died, including Lukasz Urban, the Polish driver Amri shot before seizing his vehicle. Dozens more were injured; a 13th victim died of their injuries in 2021. Amri fled the scene and made his way across Europe before being shot dead four days later by Italian police, near Milan, during a routine identity check.

"What happened behind the scenes of that attack is in many ways just as disturbing," says "Blindspot Berlin" director David Nawrath . "[It's] a picture of overwhelmed institutions, systemic failure and a staggering blindness to the threat that was developing right in front of our eyes."

Inside the Salafist network

Set in the year before the attack, the series follows police investigator Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, of "System Crasher" and "All Quiet on the Western Front") and Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla), a young officer and Arabic-language translator, as they try to infiltrate the Salafist network around Abu Walaa, the Iraqi preacher based in Hildesheim who recruited for extremist group "Islamic State" (IS). Frank recruits Murat (Tamer Trasoglu), who risks his life as an undercover informant. Inside the network, they find Amri: volatile, and getting more dangerous.

But despite repeated warnings, their bosses refuse to take the threat seriously. They dismiss Amri as a possible terrorist, in part because he is also a drug dealer, something the authorities see as incompatible with being a radical Islamist.

Fiction built on the parliamentary record

The series writers and production team closely based "Blindspot Berlin" on the facts of the Amri case, and the years-long parliamentary investigation into the institutional failures that made the attack possible. The main characters in the series — Frank, Isra and Murat — are fictionalized, but the events play out as they did in real life.

"We tried to keep as close as possible to what is known about the attack and what led to it," producer Simon Amberger told DW. "There is still a lot that isn't known, that is speculation. There we tried to leave things open."

Understaffed, uncoordinated, unheeded

The facts of the case are damning enough.

The parliamentary inquiry committee found that the criminal division investigating Amri and other suspects was grossly understaffed, that judicial and security agencies failed to coordinate the exchange of information, and that officials made serious errors of judgment. Amri's asylum claims were rejected, but he was never deported.

At one point the bureaucracy tipped into farce. Amri tried to leave Germany to rejoin his family and was stopped at the border, where police confiscated his passport on the grounds that he lacked the correct papers to go.

Not only a German story

The producers knew from the start that the story reached beyond Germany.

The Breitscheidplatz attack came at the end of a run of assaults across Europe: the Bataclan and coordinated shootings in Paris in 2015, the suicide bombings at Brussels airport and Maelbeek metro station, and a similar truck attack in Nice, in 2016.

Despite the lessons learned in the past decade, threat levels remain high. On July 25, a man drove a van into the crowds of Christopher Street Day gay pride celebrations in Berlin, killing one and injuring dozens.

The Breitscheidplatz attack also continues to resonate today, as it raises questions on "how far a free democratic society is willing to go, how much of its freedom it is willing to sacrifice for security," says Amberger.

Fears of political misuse

He's aware, however, that a story of Islamic extremism, and the failure of the German state to protect its citizens, lands differently now, in the wake of recent elections that have seen a surge of support for the anti-immigrant, Islamophobic far-right AfD party.

"There is a danger that this story, this series, could be misused to support a simplistic, populist political agenda," Amberger admits. "But it isn't that simple. [In the series] we show how extremism arises in marginalized groups that feel isolated, unseen and powerless. The solution isn't 'stop immigration.'"

"Blindspot Berlin" premieres in Germany on public broadcaster ARD in October; its international distribution is also being planned.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Von der Leyen eyes Canada as EU's first 'associate member'
entries.summary: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and Canada saw the world with the same eyes. At her annual State of the Union address, she said the bloc was dealing with an "openly hostile world."
entries.content:
Europe

Von der Leyen eyes Canada as EU's first 'associate member'

Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and Canada saw the world with the same eyes. At her annual State of the Union address, she said the bloc was dealing with an "openly hostile world."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for ‌Canada ⁠to ⁠become its first associate member — a position that the bloc would have to create from scratch.

Von der Leyen's comments came during her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, while Candanian Prime Minister Mark Carney was in attendance.

This comes days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc, a position that does not currently exist.

Earlier this week, Carney responded to the story, saying he sought a "unique alliance"with the bloc and not a membership. 

"Partnerships are a ​strategic ‌choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture ‌in the international rules-based system," ‌von ​der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union ​address.

"We see the world with the same ⁠eyes: ​from AI ​to climate change, from the Arctic ​to geopolitics. And ‌we have stood together: on Ukraine, on ​defense, ⁠on raw materials and on supply chains. ⁠But ​above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy," she said.

The EU and Canada, which have already grown close amid conflicts and trade wars, are looking to partner with each other to diversify from China and the United States respectively.

Warning against an 'openly hostile world'

Von der Leyen called for an independent European Union amid an "openly hostile world," in her speech on Wednesday. 

"'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' — this is how British author Charles Dickens described Europe in the days of the French Revolution, and it is also a fair description of the world we live in," she said, beginning her address.

"The state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been," she said.

Von der Leyen warned against "an openly hostile world" and "frayed relationships" while speaking of Russia's war against Ukraine and not directly mentioning the EU's increasingly strained relationship with the US.

"A territorial war ‌of aggression is ‌raging ​on our continent; others have erupted nearby. A ​fight for industrial capacities is shaping ⁠global ​competition. And ​a battle of ​narratives is seeking ‌to weaken confidence in ​Europe," ⁠von der Leyen said.

Von der Leyen announces new European corporation on critical raw material

Von der Leyen, now in her second five-year term as commission president, stressed on the need to maintain European independence in various sectors including energy and raw material.

"We still have too many dangerous dependencies" she said adding the EU was still 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials.

"We need to urgently procure and build up reserves. No country can do this on its own so we need to think differently," she said, hinting at global partnerships without mentioning nations.

"This is why we will establish a new European corporation on critical raw material. It will help us obtain and stockpile what we need ... Not only our industry depends on this but also our independence and security," she said.

As for China, the president warned the bloc would "use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship".

"Our trade deficit with China is now one billion euros a day. It has reached a tipping point. Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," she said. "Words are good. But deeds are better."

Future 'depends' on how EU tackles climate change, AI

Speaking of challenges, von der Leyen said the future of the 27-nation bloc depends on how it manages climate change and artificial intelligence.

"Our future prosperity and security will greatly depend on how we manage the tipping points of our time: climate change and AI," she said, promising a new "heatwave plan" following Europe's deadly summer, and a push for the bloc to help "pace the frontier" of AI development.

Social media ban for kids under 13

Von der Leyen, a mother of seven, also proposed sweeping restrictions on children's access to social media.

Under the proposal, children under 13 would be barred from accessing such platforms, while those aged 13 to 15 would be allowed to use restricted "mini accounts" supervised by a parent or guardian.

"I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree," von der Leyen said. "Each age has its own sensitivities. And therefore, each will have its own tailored protection level."

Von der Leyen is expected to formally present the legislation, known as the "KIDS Act," alongside EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen in Strasbourg on Thursday.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthis target Mecca, warns of 'red line'
entries.summary: The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses had destroyed a Houthi-deployed drone just outside Mecca, Islam's holiest city.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia says Houthis target Mecca, warns of 'red line'

Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses had destroyed a Houthi-deployed drone just outside Mecca, Islam's holiest city.

Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed a drone allegedly launched by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis before it entered restricted airspace over Islam's holiest city Mecca.

The Houthis denied targeting the city, which is the destination of the annual Muslim hajj pilgrimage.

The claim was announced by the Joint Forces Command of what is still called the Saudi-led coalition. The multinational alliance formed in 2015 has largely fragmented, leaving current operations dominated by Saudi Arabia and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said the security of Mecca and its pilgrims was a "red line" and warned that the command would take "necessary and deterrent measures."

According to the statement, the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone "launched by the Terrorist Houthi Militia."

Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and in the kingdom's southern region which borders Yemen.

How did the Houthis respond?

The Houthis were quick to reject the coalition's claims as a "lie."

"The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone," Hazem al-Assad, a high-ranking member from the Houthi movement, wrote on X.

Pakistan's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous attack on Mecca."

"The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he wrote on X.

Meanwhile, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a bloc of 57 Muslim nations, also condemned the "henious" attack.

The OIC General Secretariat "stresses that the violation of the sanctity of the holy sites is an unacceptable and intolerable transgression that requires deterring the perpetrators and blocking the path of anyone who dares to infringe upon these sites," it said in a statement.

Why are Saudi forces in conflict with the Houthis?

Saudi Arabia is being increasingly affected by the rapidly escalating conflict across its southern border in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injured 13 people on Monday night, bringing the total number of people injured since the conflict escalated in July to about 100.

In July, the Houthis also blocked Saudi oil shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

With the kingdom under attack, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday reached out to Egypt for support against Yemen's Houthi rebels. The leaders called for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

The growing escalation has opened up another front in the Middle East, which is already grappling with the US war on Iran.

Amid the latest development, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday issued an advisory asking its citizens to "reconsider travel" to the kingdom.

It warned of the "risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans and local laws regarding social media activity."

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: How hotter weather is making us poorer
entries.summary: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world.

According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties. 

These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example.

"Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers .

How climate change is already hitting incomes

A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050.

But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets? 

"If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario. 

Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains.

"Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW.

Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price.

"As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down."

Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July.

Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany.  

Compounding existing economic pressures

One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events, have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output.

Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024. 

"The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty."

The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance.

These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance.

In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality.

Can climate adaptation limit costs?

"Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study.

Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things."

However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital in order to head off much worse future economic impacts. 

The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis.

Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted.  

But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively.

Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes, can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says.

Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets.

"Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: India news: US bill sanctioning Russia could hit India with tariffs of up to 100%
entries.summary: A new bill could give President Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, potentially affecting major importer India. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India could face up to 100% US tariffs over Russian oil

Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026

A new bill could give President Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, potentially affecting major importer India. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A new bill may allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy
  • India and Russia energy ties have only strengthened since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports
  • India protests 'unacceptable and unprofessional conduct' by Pakistan Navy
  • After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Wednesday, September 16:

Skip next section After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants

After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants

Ten years after the launch of the popular instant digital payment system Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the Indian government announced charges on transactions on Tuesday.

However, the charges will only be on merchants and payments between two individuals remain free.

The charges, known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), are taking effect from October 15.

According to the government circular:

  • Person-to-person UPI payments will remain free regardless of the amount
  • Merchant payments of up to ₹2,000 (€18.06) will also remain free.
  • Merchant transactions above ₹2,000 will have 0.4% MDR levied
  • MDR will be capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more.
  • Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh (€903) a month through UPI will continue to pay zero MDR
  • Sectors such as railways, fuel and telecommunications will have a flat ₹5 fee for transactions above ₹2,000.

Last month, the Indian parliament passed a bill allowing the government to levy charges on UPI.

According to the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the MDR framework will enable further investment in "infrastructure resiliency, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service."

As of June, India had 554.9 million UPI users, according to NPCI. Meanwhile, UPI transactions worth ₹29,82,355.95 crore (about €269.3 billion) were recorded in August, NPCI data showed.

Some experts fear the new charges could prompt merchants to shift back toward cash payments.

Skip next section India protests 'unacceptable and unprofessional conduct' by Pakistan Navy

India protests 'unacceptable and unprofessional conduct' by Pakistan Navy

India on Wednesday summoned Pakistan's top diplomat to protest what it called "unacceptable and unprofessional conduct" by Pakistani naval units that led to a collision with an Indian warship in the Arabian Sea, India's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

According to India, a Pakistani naval ship approached its warship at high speed, causing a collision on Tuesday in international waters. No major damage was reported.

The Indian ship was on a routine surveillance mission, officials said.

"The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to ​convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions ​of the relevant agreements between the ‌two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," the ministry said.

India said the incident violated a 1991 agreement requiring the countries' naval vessels and submarines to maintain a distance of at least three nautical miles in international waters.

Pakistan has not issued a statement regarding the incident.

This incident marks the first overt military tension between the nuclear-armed rivals since their four-day conflict last year, which threatened to turn into a full-blown war.

Skip next section US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India

US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India

India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday.

The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month.

If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law.

The proposed tariffs seek toincrease economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.

India-US ties facing test

While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.

Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.

However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.

However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the top updates from across India.

India-US ties under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump could come under pressure as a Russia sanctions bill being debated by the US House of Representatives would allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas. This is where India comes in, as one of the major consumers of Russian energy.

Meanwhile, India's instant payment system, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), is set to be charged for the first time since its launch 10 years ago. However, the government is levying charges only on merchants, not individual users.

For all this and more, stay tuned to our live blog!
